opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most frequently asked questions in our field, and my answer may be a bit different from what people expect. Many people assume hardware is the hard part because it's physical, it's expensive, and iteration is slow. Hardware is certainly not easy. But looking at where the industry stands today, I believe software, or more precisely the intelligence, the "brain," is the real bottleneck.

Look at the past few years. Thanks to the supply chain, especially in China, the hardware for humanoid robots and mobile manipulators has improved remarkably fast. Joints, motors, reducers, dexterous hands, and batteries have all become cheaper and more reliable. You can now buy a robot body that is quite capable mechanically for a fraction of what it cost five years ago. In many demos, the hardware can already do far more than the software knows how to make it do. Teleoperate the robot and it can fold clothes, pour water, or organize shelves. That tells you the body is capable. What's missing is the autonomous intelligence to do these things on its own, in unseen environments, with high success rates.

So the gap lies in generalization. Getting a robot to perform one task in one setting is a solved engineering problem. Getting it to handle thousands of objects, varied lighting, cluttered scenes, and tasks it was never explicitly trained on is the hard part. That's fundamentally a software and data problem.

That leads to what I consider the core difficulty: data. Large language models had the entire internet to learn from. Embodied intelligence has no equivalent. There's no internet-scale corpus of robot actions. Teleoperation data is expensive and slow to collect, and it doesn't scale the way we need. That's why my team and I have put so much emphasis on synthetic data and simulation. We generate large amounts of physically realistic data in simulation, train models on it, and then transfer them to the real world. The sim-to-real gap is a real challenge, but I think this path is much more scalable than relying purely on real-world collection.

Still, I don't want to say hardware doesn't matter. Hardware and software have to co-evolve. If your software team doesn't understand the hardware, you end up designing algorithms that can't be deployed. If your hardware team doesn't understand what the model needs, you build bodies that are hard to learn on. For example, overly complex dexterous hands with many degrees of freedom may look impressive, but they can make learning and data collection much harder. Sometimes a simpler, more robust design gives you better overall performance. That's why I think full-stack capability is important for a company in this space.

So my summary: hardware is hard, but it's a known kind of hard. It's an engineering problem that the industry knows how to grind through, and the supply chain will keep driving costs down. Software, specifically general-purpose embodied intelligence, is an unknown kind of hard. It's still a scientific problem in many ways, and it's where the real breakthroughs will come from. Whoever solves generalization at scale will define the next era of this industry.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that both are hard, but they are hard in very different ways, and right now the bottleneck is clearly on the software side, specifically on the data and the models.

Let me explain why I say that. On the hardware side, if you look at a humanoid or a dexterous hand today, the components are mostly mature. Motors, reducers, sensors, batteries, the supply chain in China is very strong, and the cost is coming down fast. Hardware is hard in an engineering sense: reliability, heat, backlash, how many hours the hand can run before something wears out. These are real problems, but they are the kind of problems that engineers know how to grind down year by year. You iterate, you test, you improve. The path is visible.

Software is a different kind of hard. The question is not "how do we make it work," it is "we don't yet fully know how to make it work." A robot needs to perceive a cluttered scene, understand a task given in natural language, and then produce continuous, precise actions with its body in a physical world that pushes back. Language models got their breakthrough because the internet gave them trillions of tokens for free. Embodied intelligence has no internet of actions. Nobody uploaded a billion examples of how to fold a shirt with force feedback. So we have to create the data ourselves, through teleoperation, through simulation, through synthetic generation, and each of those has limits. That data problem is really the core of why the software is harder right now.

There is also a coupling that people underestimate. In most industries you can separate the two: build the device, then write the software. In robotics they constrain each other. If the hand has only a few degrees of freedom, no amount of clever learning will let it do fine manipulation. If the model has not seen enough data, a beautiful 20-degree-of-freedom hand is just an expensive paperweight. So when I think about difficulty, I actually think about them as one system. The hardware sets the ceiling, the software decides how close you get to it.

My own view is that generalization is the real test. Hardware that works in one factory is already valuable. Software that works in one factory is almost worthless, because the whole promise of embodied intelligence is that the same brain can walk into a new kitchen or a new warehouse and still function. That is the problem I spend most of my time on, and I think it is the one that determines whether this becomes a real industry or stays a demo.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty lies in different places. With hardware, you’re dealing with physical constraints: reliability, precision, power consumption, cost. And iteration is slow. If you discover that a mechanical design needs to change, you can’t just push an update.

Software is easier to modify, but that doesn’t mean the intelligence problem is easier. You need the robot to perceive its environment, decide what to do, and control its body in situations you didn’t anticipate. A demonstration that works once is very different from a system that works consistently in unfamiliar environments.

And the two are tightly coupled. Better hardware can simplify the software problem, while good software can compensate for some hardware limitations. So I’d look less at which one is harder in the abstract and more at what’s limiting the whole system for a particular task.

r001.rationale: The candidate says hardware and software are tightly coupled and can help compensate for each other, but does not characterize their development as progressing together in a spiral.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re difficult in different ways. Hardware has very concrete constraints: precision, reliability, cost, manufacturing, and maintenance. A robot might perform well in a demonstration, but getting it to work consistently for thousands of hours is a much harder problem. And hardware iteration is slow—you can’t fix every issue with an update.

Software faces a different challenge: the real world is open-ended. A system may work in one room with familiar objects, then fail when the lighting changes or an object is placed differently. Connecting perception, decision-making, and control in a way that generalizes is extremely difficult.

So I wouldn’t simply say hardware is harder or software is harder. It depends on what capability you’re trying to achieve and what’s currently limiting it. Better software can compensate for some hardware limitations, but it can’t create physical capabilities the robot doesn’t have. And excellent hardware alone doesn’t tell the robot what to do. The important thing is to develop them together.

r001.rationale: The candidate says hardware and software should be developed together, but does not characterize their progress as a spiral.
